questions.question: Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be a nonempty convex set and $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$. Which condition on a vector $\boldsymbol{a}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ defines $\boldsymbol{a}\in N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$, membership of the normal cone?

Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty and convex, $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$, $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ and $H_{\boldsymbol{a}}=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}\}$. Which statement about $H_{\boldsymbol{a}}$ is equivalent to $\boldsymbol{a}\in N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$?
options: $H_{\boldsymbol{a}}$ supports $V$ through $\boldsymbol{p}$, with $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}$ for all $\boldsymbol{x}\in V$.
$H_{\boldsymbol{a}}$ supports $V$ through $\boldsymbol{p}$, with $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}$ for all $\boldsymbol{x}\in V$.

questions.question: Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty and convex, $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$ and $\boldsymbol{c}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ with $\boldsymbol{c}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$. Which statement about $\boldsymbol{p}$ and the linear function $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ is equivalent to $\boldsymbol{c}\in N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$?

Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be convex and $\boldsymbol{p}\in\operatorname{Int}(V)$. Which argument shows that no $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ lies in $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$, so that $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$?
options: No hyperplane passes through an interior point of $V$, so $\boldsymbol{p}$ has no normal vector other than $\boldsymbol{0}$.
The point $\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{p}-\varepsilon\boldsymbol{a}$ lies in $V$ for small $\varepsilon>0$ and gives $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{p})<0$.
Some direction $\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{p}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ with $\boldsymbol{x}\in V$ is orthogonal to $\boldsymbol{a}$, which violates the defining inequality.
The point $\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{p}+\varepsilon\boldsymbol{a}$ lies in $V$ for small $\varepsilon>0$ and gives $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{p})>0$.

questions.question: Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty and convex, $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$, $K=\{\lambda(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{p})\colon\boldsymbol{x}\in V,\ \lambda>0\}$ and $L=\{\lambda\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{x}\in V,\ \lambda\geq0\}$. With $^{\circ}$ denoting the polar cone, which equation holds for every such $V$ and $\boldsymbol{p}$?

Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon(x_1-2)^2+(x_2-1)^2\leq5\}$, the closed disc with centre $(2,1)$ and radius $\sqrt{5}$, and let $\boldsymbol{p}=(3,3)$, a boundary point of $V$. Which vector lies in $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$?

Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1^2+x_2^2\leq1\}$, $\boldsymbol{p}=(1,0)$ and $\boldsymbol{a}=(1,1)$. Which point $\boldsymbol{x}\in V$ gives $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{p})>0$ and so shows that $\boldsymbol{a}\notin N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$?
Let $V=\{(1,2)\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$, a set consisting of one point, and $\boldsymbol{p}=(1,2)$. Which set is $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$?
Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon\lvert x_1\rvert+\lvert x_2\rvert\leq2\}$ and $\boldsymbol{p}=(1,\tfrac{1}{2})$. Which set is $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$?

Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ be convex with $\boldsymbol{p}=(3,1)\in V$, and suppose $\boldsymbol{a}=(1,2)\in N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$. Which supporting line of $V$ through $\boldsymbol{p}$, together with a halfplane containing $V$, does this give?
Let $V_1\subseteq V_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty convex sets and $\boldsymbol{p}\in V_1$. Which relation between the normal cones holds for every such $V_1$, $V_2$ and $\boldsymbol{p}$?
options: $N_{V_1}(\boldsymbol{p})=N_{V_2}(\boldsymbol{p})$ whenever $\boldsymbol{p}$ is a boundary point of both sets

questions.question: Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty and convex, not necessarily closed, and $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$. Which argument shows that $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$ is a closed convex cone?
options: It is the intersection over $\boldsymbol{x}\in V$ of the sets $\{\boldsymbol{a}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{p})\leq0\}$, each a closed convex cone.
It inherits closedness and convexity from $V$, because its defining condition runs over the points of the convex set $V$.
It is the union over $\boldsymbol{x}\in V$ of the closed half-lines $\{\lambda(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{p})\colon\lambda\geq0\}$.
It is generated by the normals $\boldsymbol{a}_i$ of finitely many linear inequalities $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b_i$ binding at $\boldsymbol{p}$.

questions.question: Let $n\geq2$, $\boldsymbol{a}\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$, $\beta\in\mathbb{R}$, let $V$ be a nonempty convex subset of the hyperplane $\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=\beta\}$, and $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$. Which statement about $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$ holds for every such $V$ and $\boldsymbol{p}$?
options: Exactly one of the vectors $\boldsymbol{a}$ and $-\boldsymbol{a}$ lies in $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$.
$N_V(\boldsymbol{p})=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$ if $V$ is a segment and $\boldsymbol{p}$ its midpoint.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3\colon x_1^2+x_2^2\leq1\}$, a solid cylinder around the $x_3$-axis with no bound on $x_3$, and let $\boldsymbol{p}=(0,1,3)$, a boundary point of $V$. Which set is $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$?
Let $V$ be the segment from $(0,0)$ to $(2,2)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\boldsymbol{p}=(2,2)$, its endpoint. Which set is $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$?

Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon0\leq x_1\leq3,\ 0\leq x_2\leq2\}$, $\boldsymbol{p}=(1,5)\notin V$, and let $\boldsymbol{q}$ be the point of $V$ nearest to $\boldsymbol{p}$. Which vector lies in $N_V(\boldsymbol{q})$?

Let $V_1,V_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be convex, $\boldsymbol{p}\in V_1\cap V_2$, and $N_{V_1}(\boldsymbol{p})+N_{V_2}(\boldsymbol{p})=\{\boldsymbol{a}_1+\boldsymbol{a}_2\colon\boldsymbol{a}_1\in N_{V_1}(\boldsymbol{p}),\ \boldsymbol{a}_2\in N_{V_2}(\boldsymbol{p})\}$. Which statement about $N_{V_1\cap V_2}(\boldsymbol{p})$ holds for all such $V_1$, $V_2$, $\boldsymbol{p}$?

Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty and convex, $\boldsymbol{c}\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$, and suppose that $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$ maximizes $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ over $V$. Which statement about $\boldsymbol{p}$ and $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$ is correct for every such $V$, $\boldsymbol{c}$ and $\boldsymbol{p}$?
options: $\boldsymbol{p}$ is the only point of $V$ at which $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ is maximal.
$\boldsymbol{p}$ is not an interior point of $V$.
If $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ is constant on $V$, $\boldsymbol{p}$ may lie in $\operatorname{Int}(V)$.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1^2+x_2^2\leq1\}$ and $\boldsymbol{p}=(0,-\sqrt{2})\notin V$. Which vector lies in $S_V(\boldsymbol{p})=\{\boldsymbol{a}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}\ \text{for all}\ \boldsymbol{x}\in V\}$?

Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1^2\leq x_2\leq1\}$ and $\boldsymbol{p}=(1,1)$, where the parabola $x_2=x_1^2$ meets the line $x_2=1$. With $\operatorname{Cone}(S)$ the set of nonnegative linear combinations of the vectors in $S$, which set is $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$?
